catalog_quote: Aussagen zum Akzent im Alur finden wir ausschließlich in Knappert ( 1963 : 70) . Dieser schreibt, daß Wurzelmorpheme den Wortakzent tragen . Hat das Wurzelmorphem die Struktur KVKV, dann liegt der Akzent auf dem ersten Vokal . In Wörtern mit der Struktur VKVKV wird der zentrale Vokal akzentuiert . Soweit befindet sich das Alur in Übereinstimmung mit den anderen südlichen Lwoo - Sprachen . Im Falle von reduplizierten Wurzeln wird keine Silbe besonders hervorgehoben bzw. in Ausnahmefällen die erste Silbe ( z . B. / ' momo / oily, abgeleitet von / ' mò / oil) . ... habe ich die Frage der Artikulation und Positionierung des Wortakzents im Alur mit einem Muttersprachler überprüft . Dabei konnte festgestellt werden, daß der Akzent durch die Erhöhung des Lungendrucks bei gleichzeitiger Längung des ihn tragenden Segments ausgedrückt wird . Die Rolle des Wurzelvokals als Akzentträger konnte mit den folgenden Beispielen bestätigt werden : / ' camo / to ... [Heusing 2006, English:] ... it is always the root vowel which carries the stress no matter whether pre- and / or suffixes are added to the root . And in example 5, which is a noun based on a disyllabic root, it is the first root vowel which carries the stress .

new_statements.translation: Statements on accent in Alur are found only in Knappert (1963: 70). He writes that root morphemes carry the word accent. If the root morpheme has the structure CVCV, the accent lies on the first vowel. In words with the structure VCVCV the central vowel is accented. [...] I checked the question of the articulation and positioning of the word accent in Alur with a native speaker. It was established that the accent is expressed by an increase of lung pressure with simultaneous lengthening of the segment that bears it. The role of the root vowel as accent bearer was confirmed with the following examples: /'camo/ to [eat] ... (Heusing 2006, p. 73f., in English: 'In examples 1-4 it is always the root vowel which carries the stress no matter whether pre- and/or suffixes are added to the root. And in example 5, which is a noun based on a disyllabic root, it is the first root vowel which carries the stress.')

new_statements.rule_in_words: Alur is a tone language (two levels H/L per Heusing; Knappert 1969 counts H, M, L) with a non-distinctive, bound dynamic word accent that sits on the root morpheme: the (first) root vowel carries it regardless of prefixes or suffixes (/'cam-o/ 'to eat', /ê-'cám-é/ 'he eats it', /'gak-írí/ 'to avoid each other', /'dhógól-á/ 'door'); CVCV roots accent the first vowel, VCVCV words the central vowel. Loanwords keep the stress position of the donor language (/sù'kúru/ 'school', /daki'tár/ 'doctor', /senthì'méthrì/ 'centimetre'). Knappert 1969 describes the same root prominence as vowel lengthening and says intensity stress is 'not significant'; Heusing's native-speaker check found raised pulmonary pressure plus lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any snippet examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplicated roots: no syllable especially prominent, or exceptionally the first syllable (/'momo/ 'oily' < /'mò/ 'oil'); in the reconstruction section Heusing states that in Alur, Adhola and Luo the accent of reduplicated forms falls on the first vowel (the vowel of the reduplicated part), against Acholi/Kumam/Lango (second vowel). Loanwords retain donor-language stress (English, Swahili; a Swahili penultimate-stress form is used to argue direct borrowing from Swahili rather than Arabic) and usually carry a falling tone on the syllable stressed in the source language (Heusing 2004 §3.2, data from Ukoko/Knappert/Spaandonck 1964).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root morpheme + affixes) in cognate vocabulary and in loanwords; accent has no distinctive/grammatical function but conditions tone sandhi (Heusing 2004: 157; Storch 2005 §4.3). Heusing's synchronic data are from Western (Congo) Alur samples and one native-speaker consultant; Knappert's data are Congo (Mahagi) Dho-Alur. Access caveat: all quotations are verbatim scanned fragments returned by the public Google Books feed for books without page preview, saved to disk; the full text has not been read.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Alur proper (alur1250 / alz). Heusing 2004 separates West-Alur (DR Congo, Mahagi side) and Ost-Alur (Uganda) for some consonant features; Storch notes his samples are Western Alur, and his native-speaker accent check does not name the dialect. Knappert 1962/1963/1969 and the 1964 Ghent dictionary describe Congo (Mahagi) Dho-Alur; Ringe 1953 is Ugandan Alur. No separate glottocode for these dialects (Jonam, Jokot, Mambisa, Wanyoro are listed as subdialects on Wikipedia).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Heusing 2004 statement (root morpheme carries the word accent; first vowel of a KVKV root), so it agrees on the root-stress reading; it refines it by stating explicitly that affixes never take stress, that the first root vowel is stressed in polysyllabic roots, that the pattern is reconstructed for Proto-South-Lwoo, and that loanwords keep their donor-language stress position (penultimate or final in the Swahili and English examples), which is an exception to the root rule. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field, so this work supplies a rule where the catalog has none.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is bound to the root: the root vowel carries it whatever prefixes or suffixes are attached; in the rare polysyllabic (noun) roots the first, leftmost root vowel is stressed (Table 10: /'cam-o/ 'to eat', /ê-'cám-él/ 'he eats it', /'gak-írí/ 'to avoid each other', /'dhógól-á/ 'door'). Heusing treats this as inherited from a reconstructed Proto-South-Lwoo bound root stress and refers to Heusing (2004: 157-165) for detail.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the snippets read.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords: 'Loanwords, on the other hand, seem to have been borrowed into Proto-South-Lwoo together with their inherent stress patterns. Again, Alur retained this strategy [..] The inherent stress position of the loanword is always retained in Alur no matter from which donor language the loanword is received (in the examples it is English or Swahili).' Table 11: /sù'kúru/ 'school', /senthì'méthrì/ 'centimetre', /daki'tár/ 'doctor' (< Swahili dak'tari), /sù'karı/ 'sugar' (< Swahili su'kari, penult stress, which Heusing uses to show the word came from Swahili rather than Arabic). Loanwords are said to be marked as such by 'segmental and suprasegmental elements'; the paper also notes a falling tone on the syllable 'which carries stress in the donor language', while 'falling tones in Southern Lwoo cognates' are always derived by deletion or derivation. The in-text cross-references say 'Table 13' and 'Table 14' where the captions read 'Table 10' and 'Table 11'.
new_statements.identity_note: Heusing 2006 describes Alur as spoken in Uganda/DR Congo from the author's own fieldwork on loanwords; no particular dialect is named in the snippets read. The paper explicitly frames the stress rule as Southern Lwoo-wide (reconstructed for Proto-South-Lwoo) and retained in Alur.

new_statements.quote: 3.5. Stress pattern In addition to segmental peculiarities also stress patterns can help to identify loanwords in Alur. For Proto-South-Lwoo, a bound stress has been reconstructed which is carried by the root vowel of a word. If a root has more than one syllable (which is rare and restricted to nouns [...] first root vowel (i.e. the one to the extreme left) serves as carrier for the stress. Alur has retained these stress patterns in cognates as you can easily see in Table 13. [...] Loanwords, on the other hand, seem to have been borrowed into Proto-South-Lwoo together with their inherent stress patterns. Again, Alur retained this strategy as can be seen in Table 14. The inherent stress position of the loanword is always retained in Alur no matter from which donor language the loanword is received (in the examples it is English or Swahili).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Native (cognate) Alur words carry a bound word stress on the root vowel regardless of prefixes/suffixes; in the rare polysyllabic (noun) roots the first (leftmost) root vowel is stressed (Table 10/13: 'cam-o, ê-'cám-él, 'gak-o, 'gak-írí, 'dhógól-á). Loanwords are the exception: they keep the stress position of the donor language (Table 11/14: sù'kúru 'school', senthì'méthrì 'centimetre', daki'tár 'doctor' < Sw. dak'tari, sù'karı 'sugar' < Sw. su'kari, i.e. penultimate/final as in the source), which the author uses as a diagnostic for borrowing.

new_statements.identity_note: Alur (dho-Alur), Western Nilotic, Southern Lwoo; Heusing's data are from Ugandan Alur fieldwork (per Heusing 2004) and the paper treats Alur as a whole without naming a dialect in the snippets seen.
